title: Lightning Web Components
description: Modern JavaScript to production-ready components: templates, events, data, lifecycle, styling, testing, accessibility and security.

nodes.title: Modern JavaScript
nodes.summary: Modules, classes, arrow functions, promises and async/await.
nodes.lesson:
Lightning web components are plain modern JavaScript. Before LWC, be comfortable with:

- `const` and `let`, template literals, destructuring and the spread operator (`[...items, next]`).
- **Modules**: `import` and `export`; each component is a module.
- **Classes** with fields, getters and methods; `this` inside them.
- **Arrow functions**, which keep the surrounding `this`.
- **Promises** and `async`/`await` for anything that takes time, like a server call; `try`/`catch` for their errors.
- Array methods: `map`, `filter`, `find`, `reduce`, and why they return new arrays instead of changing the old one.
concepts: map, filter and reduce return new arrays
pitfalls: Mutating an array in place (`push`) and expecting a re-render: reassign instead.
Forgetting `await`, then working with a pending Promise.

quiz.q: Which creates a new array with one more item, leaving the old one unchanged?
quiz.why: Spread copies the array into a new one; push changes the original.

quiz.q: What does `await` do inside an async function?
options: Waits for a Promise to settle and gives its value
quiz.why: await pauses the function until the Promise resolves (or throws if it rejects).

quiz.q: Why do LWC handlers often use arrow functions?
options: They keep `this` from the surrounding code
quiz.why: Arrow functions don't rebind `this`.

nodes.title: Tools and local setup
nodes.summary: VS Code, the Salesforce CLI, and where components live.
nodes.lesson:
- Components live in `force-app/main/default/lwc/<name>/`: `name.html`, `name.js`, optional `name.css`, and `name.js-meta.xml`, which says where the component can be used (record page, app page, Experience site…) and with which properties.
- Create one with `sf lightning generate component --type lwc --name myThing`, deploy with `sf project deploy start`.
- Component folder names are **camelCase**; in markup they become **kebab-case**: `<c-my-thing>`.
- SFCode's LWC problems run your component in a sandboxed browser frame, so you can practise without an org.
concepts: Component folder structure and the js-meta.xml file
Targets: where a component can be placed
pitfalls: Forgetting to expose the component (`isExposed` and targets) in js-meta.xml, so it doesn't appear in Lightning App Builder.

quiz.q: A component's folder is `accountCard`. How do you use it in another template?
quiz.why: Namespace `c`, kebab-case name.

quiz.q: Which file decides where a component can be placed in Lightning App Builder?
quiz.why: js-meta.xml holds isExposed and targets.

quiz.q: Which command deploys your components to an org?
quiz.why: Components are metadata and deploy like any other source.

nodes.title: Your first component
nodes.lesson: A component is a class and a template: ```js import { LightningElement, api } from "lwc"; export default class Greeting extends LightningElement { @api name = "World"; // public: a parent can set it count = 0; // private and reactive increment() { this.count += 1; } } ``` ```html ``` - Every field is **reactive**: reassign it and the template re-renders. - `@api` marks public properties (and methods) that a parent can use. - Handlers are passed by name (`onclick={increment}`), not called.
pitfalls: Calling the handler in the template (`onclick={increment()}`).
Changing an @api property from inside the component: the parent owns it.

nodes.title: Templates and rendering
nodes.summary: Lists, conditions, getters and dynamic classes.
nodes.lesson: Templates bind data but can't compute, so logic goes in **getters**: - **Lists**: ``; every item needs a unique `key`. - **Conditions**: ``. - **Getters** compute what to show: `get hasItems() { return this.items.length > 0; }`, and recompute on each render. - **Dynamic classes and attributes**: `class={rowClass}` where a getter returns `"row selected"`. - `lwc:ref` gives you an element without querying for it.
concepts: Getters for derived values and classes
pitfalls: Using the array index as the key: re-ordering then confuses rendering.
Expressions in templates (`{count > 0}`) don't work: use a getter.

nodes.title: Styling and SLDS
nodes.summary: Shadow DOM, SLDS and styling hooks.
nodes.lesson:
- Component CSS is **scoped**: styles in `myThing.css` only reach that component's own template, thanks to the **shadow DOM**.
- The **Salesforce Lightning Design System (SLDS)** gives Salesforce's look: utility classes like `slds-p-around_medium` and blueprints for common patterns.
- To customise base components from outside, use **styling hooks** (CSS custom properties such as `--slds-c-button-brand-color-background`), not selectors that reach inside them.
- Theme with variables so the component follows the org's branding.
concepts: Scoped CSS and the shadow DOM
pitfalls: Trying to style inside a base component with deep selectors: shadow DOM blocks it; use styling hooks.
Hard-coding colours that clash with the org's theme.

quiz.q: Why doesn't a CSS rule in a parent change the inside of a child component?
options: Shadow DOM scopes each component's styles
quiz.why: Each component's styles are encapsulated.

quiz.q: How do you change a lightning-button's brand colour?
quiz.why: Styling hooks are the supported way to customise base components.

quiz.q: What does SLDS provide?
options: Salesforce's design system: CSS classes and patterns
quiz.why: SLDS is the CSS and design guidance for the Salesforce look.

nodes.title: Events
nodes.summary: Children talk to parents with CustomEvents.
nodes.lesson:
Data flows **down** as properties; changes flow **up** as **events**:

```js
this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("select", { detail: { id: this.recordId } }));
```

```html
<c-tile onselect={handleSelect}></c-tile>
```

- Event names are lower-case, with no `on` prefix; the parent listens with `on` + the name.
- Pass data in `detail`; keep it simple (primitives or plain copies).
- `bubbles: true` lets the event travel up through ancestors; `composed: true` lets it leave the shadow boundary. Use them only when needed.
concepts: Lower-case event names; `on` + name in the parent
pitfalls: camelCase event names that never match the listener.
Passing a live object in detail that the parent then mutates.

nodes.title: Lifecycle hooks
nodes.lesson:
Components go through a lifecycle, and each hook has a job:

- `constructor()`: set up fields. Don't read attributes or touch the DOM.
- `connectedCallback()`: the component is in the page: load data, subscribe to channels, start timers.
- `renderedCallback()`: runs after **every** render; work with the DOM here, and guard with a flag so you don't trigger endless re-renders.
- `disconnectedCallback()`: unsubscribe and clear timers, or they leak.
- `errorCallback(error, stack)`: on a parent, catches errors from children, like an error boundary.
concepts: What belongs in connectedCallback versus renderedCallback
pitfalls: Setting a field in renderedCallback without a guard: infinite render loop.
Subscribing in connectedCallback but never unsubscribing.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. Where do you subscribe to a message channel?
quiz.why: Subscribe once the component is in the page; unsubscribe in disconnectedCallback.
quiz.imageAlt: Lifecycle diagram: connectedCallback is labelled 'Inserted into the page: load data, subscribe'.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, which hook runs after every render?
quiz.why: renderedCallback runs after each render, so guard work inside it.
quiz.imageAlt: Lifecycle diagram: renderedCallback is labelled 'After every render'.

quiz.q: What should disconnectedCallback do?
quiz.why: Clean up so nothing keeps running after the component is gone.

nodes.diagramCaption: LWC lifecycle: constructor, connectedCallback when inserted, render, renderedCallback after every render, disconnectedCallback when removed; errorCallback catches errors in children.

nodes.title: Lightning Data Service
nodes.summary: Reading and saving records with security and caching built in.
nodes.lesson:
**Lightning Data Service (LDS)** reads and writes records without Apex:

- `lightning-record-form`, `lightning-record-view-form` and `lightning-record-edit-form` build forms with sharing and field-level security applied.
- `getRecord` (with `@wire`) and `updateRecord` / `createRecord` from `lightning/uiRecordApi` work with single records in code.
- LDS keeps one **shared cache**: when one component updates a record, every component showing it refreshes.
- Prefer LDS for single records; use Apex for queries across many records.
pitfalls: Writing Apex to fetch one record by Id: LDS does it with security and caching.
Importing fields by string instead of schema imports, so renames aren't caught.

resources.title: Lightning Web Components and Salesforce Data (Trailhead)

quiz.q: Two components show the same record; one updates it with updateRecord. What happens to the other?
options: It refreshes from the shared LDS cache
quiz.why: LDS shares one cache per record.

quiz.q: Which base component builds an edit form with field-level security applied?
quiz.why: Record forms use LDS, which respects FLS and sharing.

quiz.q: When is Apex the better choice than LDS?
quiz.why: LDS works with single records; lists and complex queries need Apex (or the list APIs).

nodes.title: Calling Apex
nodes.summary: @wire versus imperative calls, caching and refreshApex.
pitfalls: DML in a cacheable method: it fails.
Forgetting refreshApex, so the list stays stale.
Assuming the UI hides data: the Apex method returns whatever it queries.

quiz.q: Which Apex methods can be used with @wire?
quiz.why: Wired Apex must be cacheable.

quiz.q: What does `$recordId` in a wire's parameters mean?
options: A reactive reference: the wire re-runs when recordId changes
quiz.why: The $ prefix makes the parameter reactive.

quiz.q: A list is wired; you update a contact imperatively. What refreshes the list?
quiz.why: refreshApex re-runs the wired call.

nodes.title: Talking across the page
nodes.summary: Lightning Message Service and the pub-sub pattern.
nodes.lesson:
Components that aren't parent and child, or LWC talking to Aura and Visualforce on the same page, use **Lightning Message Service (LMS)**:

1. Define a **message channel** (`MyChannel__c.messageChannel-meta.xml`).
2. Publish: `publish(this.messageContext, CHANNEL, { recordId })`.
3. Subscribe in `connectedCallback`, unsubscribe in `disconnectedCallback`.

Use events for parent and child, LMS for unrelated components. Don't use LMS just to avoid passing a property.
pitfalls: Forgetting to unsubscribe: handlers keep firing after the component is gone.
Reaching for LMS between a parent and its own child.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. Two components with no parent-child link need to share a selected record. How?
quiz.why: Unrelated components publish and subscribe on a message channel.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: c-child publishes to a Message channel and c-unrelated subscribes to it.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, how does data reach c-child from c-parent?
quiz.why: Data flows down through @api properties.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: an arrow labelled '@api props down' from c-parent to c-child.

quiz.q: Can LMS reach Aura components and Visualforce pages on the same Lightning page?
quiz.why: LMS works across LWC, Aura and Visualforce on a Lightning page.

nodes.diagramCaption: LWC communication: properties down, events up, and a Lightning Message Service channel between unrelated components.

nodes.title: Navigation and feedback
nodes.lesson:
- **NavigationMixin** moves the user without hard-coded URLs: `this[NavigationMixin.Navigate]({ type: "standard__recordPage", attributes: { recordId, actionName: "view" } })`.
- **Toasts** confirm or warn: dispatch `ShowToastEvent` with a title, message and variant.
- **LightningModal** opens a dialog component and returns a result when it closes.
- Hard-coded URLs break across orgs, sandboxes, Experience sites and mobile; the mixin works everywhere.
pitfalls: Building links with string URLs like `/lightning/r/...`: they break in Experience sites and mobile.

quiz.q: How do you open a record page from a component?
quiz.why: The mixin builds the right URL for the current context.

quiz.q: Which shows a short confirmation like 'Contact saved'?
quiz.why: Toasts give brief feedback.

quiz.q: Why avoid hard-coded URLs?
options: They break across orgs, Experience sites and mobile
quiz.why: Page references adapt to where the component runs.

nodes.title: Jest tests
concepts: createElement and appending to the document
pitfalls: Checking the DOM straight after a change, before it re-renders.
Tests that depend on each other because the DOM isn't cleaned between them.

quiz.q: Where do you query a component's rendered elements in Jest?
quiz.why: The component's DOM is in its shadow root.

quiz.q: You set a property then check the text immediately and it's stale. Why?
options: Re-rendering is asynchronous: await a microtask first
Properties can't be set in tests
quiz.why: Wait for the re-render, e.g. `await Promise.resolve()`.

quiz.q: How do tests handle a wired Apex method?
options: Mock the adapter and emit test data
quiz.why: Jest tests never reach an org; adapters are mocked.

nodes.title: Accessibility and performance
nodes.summary: Keyboard, ARIA, and keeping components fast.
nodes.lesson:
- Use real elements: `<button>` for actions, `<a>` for navigation, labels on every input. Base components handle most of this for you.
- **Keyboard**: everything clickable must be reachable with Tab and work with Enter/Space; custom widgets (tabs, menus) follow ARIA patterns with arrow keys.
- **ARIA** fills gaps: `aria-selected`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-live` for updates. Don't add ARIA where native semantics already exist.
- **Performance**: render only what's visible, avoid heavy work in getters (they run every render), cache server results, and lazy-load rarely used parts.
concepts: Cheap getters, caching and lazy loading
pitfalls: Clickable `<div>`s with no keyboard support.
Expensive loops in getters that run on every render.

quiz.q: A row of tabs must work with the keyboard. Which roles do they need?
quiz.why: The ARIA tabs pattern uses tablist, tab and tabpanel with aria-selected.

quiz.q: Why keep getters cheap?
quiz.why: Getters recompute each render, so heavy work slows the component.

quiz.q: What should you use for an action a user clicks?
quiz.why: Buttons are focusable and keyboard-accessible by default.

nodes.title: Security in components
nodes.summary: Lightning Web Security, safe DOM work and trusted data.
nodes.lesson:
- **Lightning Web Security** (and Lightning Locker before it) isolates components by namespace: one can't read another's DOM or globals.
- Avoid `innerHTML` with data; let the template render text, which escapes it. If you must render HTML, use `lightning-formatted-rich-text`.
- Third-party libraries load as **static resources** with `loadScript`; the Content Security Policy blocks scripts from arbitrary sites unless an admin trusts them.
- Every `@AuraEnabled` method is an API: enforce sharing and field access in Apex.
concepts: Lightning Web Security and namespace isolation
Rendering text safely instead of innerHTML
Static resources and CSP trusted sites
pitfalls: Setting innerHTML from record data: a script-injection risk.
Loading a library from a CDN URL, blocked by CSP.

quiz.q: How should a component show user-entered text?
options: Bind it in the template ({text}), which escapes it
quiz.why: Template bindings render text safely.

quiz.q: How do you use a third-party JavaScript library?
options: A script tag to a CDN
Upload it as a static resource and loadScript it
Paste it into an Apex class
quiz.why: Static resources plus loadScript work within the platform's CSP.

quiz.q: What stops a component from reading another namespace's DOM?
quiz.why: LWS isolates components by namespace.

nodes.title: LWC checkpoint
nodes.summary: Practise the PD I user-interface section.
nodes.lesson: You can now build, connect, style, test and secure Lightning web components. Practise the **User Interface** section of the PD I questions, and try the LWC problems you haven't solved. JavaScript-heavy roles may also want the **JavaScript Developer I** certification.
concepts: Putting events, data, lifecycle and testing together
pitfalls: Skipping tests because the component 'looks right' in the browser.
